visible.summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for this province. That absence records the absence of documented divergence — not local safety: the province remains governed by the same blanket national rules documented below.

Those rules: a judicial package leaked in October 2025 would criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality (up to three years) and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to four); raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare from 18 to 25 behind a permanent-infertility mandate with state-hospital evaluations; and expose patients (up to three years) and providers (up to seven) to charges — protested by 15 LGBTI groups and the national medical association, against regional-court precedent. The country's longest-running LGBTI monitor's 2025 report finds hostility become explicit state policy: 'family' directives, the first closure of an LGBTI organisation in years, 6 right-to-life violations (3 hate-motivated killings), 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, 313 liberty violations with 299 detention decisions, and expression violations rising from 216 to 540. In July 2025 police ran mass identity-check roundups detaining trans women, recording names and images without stated legal grounds.
visible.tangentialFactors: The draft judicial package's same-sex-ceremony and 'promotion' offences, and nationwide 'Year of the Family' rainbow-symbol bans enforced through public institutions, are LGB-adjacent instruments that shape how police treat gender-nonconforming people here too.
visible.localsOnly: Gender-marker registration through the civil registry, the restricted gender-affirming-care pathway, and the placement of trans detainees in men's facilities are resident-facing processes; visitors do not interact with them.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): HRW news release, Oct 29, 2025, reports the leaked omnibus draft ("11th Judicial Package") that would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" (up to three years in prison) and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to four years), and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison and patients up to three years, with possible pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; HRW warns it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

National-framework monitoring report (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): Kaos GL's 2025 review ("The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People") finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy — "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions and the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, with expression and artistic freedom restricted and events cancelled or banned. It documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings (trans people the most affected), 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (up from 51 the prior year), 313 liberty violations — about two and a half times the previous year — with 299 detention decisions, private-life violations rising from 16 to 67 including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy, and 61 travel bans.

visible.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): BC: consistently Canada's most progressive province on LGBT issues (first human-rights code inclusion 1992); Vancouver Davie Village scene. Regional evidence: no hostile provincial legislation, but a documented 2023 wave of coordinated disruptions against public drag-storytime events at libraries — Coquitlam Public Library postponed/cancelled repeatedly (Jan 14 2023 protest at the Town Centre branch; Oct 13 2023 postponement) under "public safety risk" claims, with a counter-gathering becoming the largest queer gathering the Tri-Cities had seen; at a Richmond library event with no police on scene a man pushed through to photograph the performer; a Granville Island children's drag camp was threatened and required a public rally of support. Scored relative to the national score (0.86) for Canada.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2023 library drag-storytime disruption wave targets gender-nonconforming expression broadly (drag performers, children's events), not trans identity specifically; documented police non-presence at a Richmond incident signals thin protection for any gender-nonconforming visitor in comparable settings.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The national police-reported hate-crime statistics (658 sexual-orientation incidents in 2024) mix LGB and trans motivations and carry no provincial breakdown - treat as national climate context, not evidence of BC-specific risk.

sources.claim: Statistics Canada 'The Daily' release (30 March 2026) on police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024: 4,882 hate crimes reported, +1% from 2023 (which had risen 34% from 2022), more than doubling (+169%) since 2018; the rate per 100,000 population fell 2% to 11.9 incidents. Incidents targeting sexual orientation declined 26% to 658, while religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. No British Columbia-specific figures appear in the release (national context only).
NOTE: not retrievable at fetch time (HTTP 307 redirect loop); the underlying Egale Canada report analyses 2024 hate-crime data affecting 2SLGBTQI people in Canada.

Canada's national framework (which applies in British Columbia under section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms) protects LGBTQ people from discrimination based on sexual orientation; sexual orientation has been covered federally since 1996 and gender identity and gender expression are protected under the Criminal Code hate-propaganda and anti-discrimination provisions. A 2021 Criminal Code amendment, in force since 2022, made Canada the first country in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults, and transgender people may change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. The record's claim of no hostile provincial legislation and its national baseline score of 0.86 stand on this framework: Charter equality protection, nationwide conversion-therapy criminalisation, and legal gender change availability in every province including BC.

visible.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Valparaíso/Viña: Chile's bohemian port-university culture; criminality is general rather than gender-targeted. Regional evidence: by a wide margin the country's highest-incidence region for anti-LGBTI discrimination - in 2024 it concentrated 51.32% of all national recorded cases (Metropolitana second at 25.12%), up 80.93% over 2023. In 2025 recorded cases fell here alongside Metropolitana while all 14 other regions rose; Movilh reads this as a decentralisation of hate toward territories with less LGBTIQ visibility and debate, not a local improvement. Scored relative to the national score (0.72) for Chile.
visible.tangentialFactors: National-level hostility climate reaching the region: a parliamentary commission approved a report in May 2025 framing gender-affirming care for youth as harmful (recommending hormone bans for minors), giving political weight to stigmatising narratives that shape public hostility a visitor may encounter.
visible.localsOnly: Resident-facing: the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) was excluded from the 2026 budget, cutting a national transition-care pathway; self-determination legal gender recognition is a national procedure.

sources.claim: Outright International country page (12 March 2026): same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; since 2012 Chile's hate-crime law has included sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances and same-sex civil unions have been recognised since 2015; a 2019 comprehensive legal gender-recognition law is based on self-determination, and a third sex option has been available for intersex children on birth certificates since 2006. No legal ban exists on medically unnecessary interventions on minors, though the Health Minister published non-binding intersex-affirming guidance in 2023; a 2020 family-court decision recognised two women as parents of a child born through assisted reproduction and a 2025 criminal court issued the country's first conviction in the field. National-framework source kept per rule 5: the record claims the national score and no region-specific source covers the national framework this pass.

Movilh XXIV Annual Human Rights Report on sexual and gender diversity in Chile (published March 2026, covering 2025): Valparaíso concentrated 51.32% of national recorded anti-LGBTI discrimination cases in 2024, up 80.93% over 2023; in 2025 cases fell only in Valparaíso and Metropolitana while all other regions rose - Movilh reads this as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ themes have less visibility; full per-region and per-commune series 2002-2025.

Wikipedia's Chile country overview is the national framework a visitor to Región de Valparaíso stands under: the 2012 Zamudio anti-discrimination law protects sexual orientation and gender identity, civil unions have been recognised since 2015, and same-sex marriage with full adoption rights has been legal since March 2022. Gender Identity Law 21.120 (introduced 2013, enacted 2018) has since 2019 let transgender people aged 14 and over change their name and gender on all official documents without surgery, and the armed forces admit LGBT personnel. Until 2022 Article 365 of the Penal Code set a higher age of consent of 18 for male homosexual acts; the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in a 5-5 vote in August 2018, and it was abolished by Law 21,483 in August 2022, equalising the age of consent.

Spanish Wikipedia's overview of sexual diversity in Chile carries four items directly relevant to this region: the first Encuentro de Oficinas Municipales de Diversidad (gathering of municipal diversity offices) was held in 2022 in Valparaíso (the second in 2023 in Melipilla, the third in 2024 in Concepción); San Antonio, in Región de Valparaíso, was among the founding comunas of the Red de Municipalidades por la Diversidad, Inclusión y No Discriminación ('Red Diversa') created in 2014, a network of municipalities with LGBTIQA+ offices or programmes that had grown beyond 60 municipalities by 2024; in April 2016 the first Carabinero contracted a civil union with a same-sex partner; and in 2020 the Chilean Army formally incorporated its first transgender member. The same page confirms the national baseline: Ley Zamudio (2012) against discrimination, same-sex marriage under Ley 21.400 (promulgated 9 December 2021, in force 10 March 2022), and Ley 21.430 (2022) banning discrimination based on sex characteristics for children and adolescents.

visible.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Dijon / Cote-d'Or: rural traditional department. Regional evidence: the only prefecture in the country found to have twice banned a Pride march from its city centre with the ban upheld - on 12 June 2025 the prefecture prohibited the Pride 2025 march in central Dijon citing "risk of trouble to public order", the second consecutive year of the same restriction; the organisers' withdrawal citing LGBT visibility was itself called significant by the city. On 14 June 2025 the administrative court rejected the legal challenge, and the march (about 1,500 people per police) proceeded on a diverted route around the historic centre; the prefecture justified the ban by estimated organiser numbers (200 vs previous 2,500 and 1,500 turnouts) and a stated risk of violent individuals attaching themselves. The march itself passed peacefully ("joyful and festive, without a hitch") - the harm documented here is the restriction and its chilling effect, not violence. Scored relative to the national score (0.67) for France.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2025 Pride-march bans were motivated by broad public-order reasoning against an LGB-allies-and-trans community march rather than any trans-specific measure; their chilling effect reaches gender-nonconforming visibility in public spaces broadly, which is how a trans visitor may encounter them.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018): trans women incarcerated in the country on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal grey area and are punished beyond their alleged crimes - placement problems in the prison system. National prison-system context (not prefecture-specific).

The national detention ombuds's opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: based on about 40 referrals since 2010, finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across all places of detention; recommendations also apply to intersex and non-binary persons. National prison-system context.

Wikipedia's national 'LGBTI en France' page is the framework document every French region, Bourgogne-Franche-Comté included, stands under: the law of 17 May 2013 opened marriage to same-sex couples, and the article details legal protections against discrimination while stating that LGBT people continue to be the target of discrimination and violence, with reports of such incidents rising. Its transidentité section covers the legal framework for gender recognition in France. This supplies the national legal baseline (marriage, anti-discrimination law, gender recognition) that applies identically in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, against which the region's own documented restriction (the Dijon Pride march ban) is an exception rather than the rule.

This page on Pride marches in France documents, citing France 3 Bourgogne, that from 2013 pride marches were organised in the Bourgogne cities of Chalon-sur-Saône, Dijon and Auxerre - i.e., the Dijon march that the Côte-d'Or prefecture banned from the city centre in June 2025 was an established regional event with over a decade of local history, not a first-time gathering. The page also records the nationwide growth of marches since the mid-1990s (with marches spreading to provincial cities from 1994-1995 onward), providing the French regional context in which the Dijon restriction occurred.
